    Fellers, et al v. Kelley, et al (opens in a new tab)
    Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-ca1-25-01442 / USCOURTS-ca1-25-01442-0

    FAPD-AI: The First Circuit reviewed an appeal of a district court's denial of a preliminary injunction sought by parents and a grandparent who were ordered by Bow High School officials in New Hampshire to remove pink "XX" wristbands they wore as a passive protest at a girls' soccer game on September 17, 2024, where a transgender athlete participated. The appellants asserted the school district violated the First Amendment through viewpoint discrimination via these sanctions and restrictions on future attendance at athletic events. The court found the appellants likely succeeded on their viewpoint discrimination claim and remanded the case to the district court for further proceedings. USCOURTS-SEL-01

    Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-ca3-24-02830 / USCOURTS-ca3-24-02830-0

    FAPD-AI: Three New Jersey hospitals appealed the dismissal of claims against Cigna for underpaying healthcare services provided to Cigna subscribers between 2016 and 2021 under the Employee Retirement Income Security Act.     FAPD-AI: The Tenth Circuit affirmed the Board of Immigration Appeals' denial of Morees Harmez's fifth motion to reopen his removal proceedings. Harmez, an Iraqi refugee with lawful permanent resident status who was ordered removed due to a felony drug conviction, sought reopening based on alleged changed conditions for Christians in Iraq and claimed eligibility for Convention Against Torture protection. The court found that the evidence did not demonstrate a material change in country conditions since his first motion in 2017, and that Harmez failed to establish a prima facie case for Convention Against Torture protection. USCOURTS-SEL-01

  • Observed at 17:10:57 Eastern time ET
    Civica Simpson v. Jessica Recksiedler, et al (opens in a new tab)
    Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-ca11-25-12318 / USCOURTS-ca11-25-12318-0

    FAPD-AI: Civica Simpson, a pro se plaintiff, appealed the dismissal of her corrected second amended complaint that named 33 defendants including judges, sheriffs, and state officials and alleged violations of federal and state constitutional rights under various statutes. The district court dismissed the complaint as a shotgun pleading under Federal Rules of Civil Procedure 8 and 10 because it contained conclusory allegations, failed to separate claims by defendant, and did not specify which defendant was responsible for which conduct. The Eleventh Circuit affirmed the dismissal with prejudice, finding the district court did not abuse its discretion. USCOURTS-SEL-01

  • Observed at 17:10:57 Eastern time ET
    USA v. Christopher Messer (opens in a new tab)
    Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-ca11-25-12745 / USCOURTS-ca11-25-12745-0

    FAPD-AI: Christopher Shaw Messer appealed his sentence of 112 months imprisonment for possession with intent to distribute at least 50 grams of methamphetamine, arguing the sentence was substantively unreasonable and below the guideline range of 188 to 235 months. The government moved to dismiss the appeal based on an appeal waiver in Messer's plea agreement that he signed and acknowledged understanding during the plea colloquy. The Eleventh Circuit granted the government's motion and dismissed the appeal, finding the waiver was made knowingly and voluntarily and enforceable. USCOURTS-SEL-01

  • Observed at 17:10:57 Eastern time ET
    USA v. Richard Colvin (opens in a new tab)
    Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-ca11-25-13002 / USCOURTS-ca11-25-13002-0

    FAPD-AI: Richard Colvin appealed his conviction for transmitting a threatening phone call in interstate commerce, challenging the jury instruction on mental state, the exclusion of mental health evidence, and the admission of lay witness testimony from a phone company employee. The Eleventh Circuit affirmed the conviction, holding that although the jury instruction may have required a higher mental state (knowledge) than the minimum recklessness standard established in Counterman v. Colorado, the error was harmless because it actually required the government to prove more culpable conduct. USCOURTS-SEL-01

  • Observed at 17:10:57 Eastern time ET
    Access Point Financial, LLC v. Charles Everhardt (opens in a new tab)
    Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-ca11-26-11169 / USCOURTS-ca11-26-11169-0

    FAPD-AI: Access Point Financial sued Charles Everhardt to enforce personal liability under a guaranty agreement for approximately $3 million in remaining debt after the foreclosure of properties securing a $56.33 million loan to three entities he managed. The district court granted summary judgment for Access Point, finding that two full recourse events under the guaranty triggered Everhardt's personal liability: the voluntary Chapter 11 bankruptcy filing by Houston Borrower and the change in management to DDI without Access Point's consent. The Eleventh Circuit affirmed, holding that the Guaranty did not require an authorized filing and that Georgia law required construction strongly against the guarantor. USCOURTS-SEL-01

  • Observed at 17:10:56 Eastern time ET
    Harold Dombrowski v. Wilson, et al (opens in a new tab)
    Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-ca11-25-10034 / USCOURTS-ca11-25-10034-0

    FAPD-AI: Harold Dombrowski, an inmate at Hamilton Correctional Facility, slipped and fell while working as a kitchen cook without required safety boots, fracturing his hip and requiring replacement surgery. He sued three prison officials under the Eighth Amendment, alleging they violated his rights by refusing to provide boots and delaying medical treatment after his fall. The court affirmed summary judgment for the officials, finding no evidence they were subjectively aware of a substantial risk of serious harm from the lack of boots or that they caused the delay in treatment. USCOURTS-SEL-01

  • Observed at 17:10:56 Eastern time ET
    USA v. Julio Rodriguez (opens in a new tab)
    Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-ca11-25-10615 / USCOURTS-ca11-25-10615-0

    FAPD-AI: Julio Rodriguez, serving a life sentence for drug trafficking and robbery conspiracy convictions imposed in 2003, sought compassionate release under 18 U.S.C. § 3582(c)(1)(A), arguing he had been rehabilitated and noting the government no longer prosecutes reverse sting operations like the one for which he was convicted. The district court denied his motion, citing his extensive violent criminal history and numerous disciplinary infractions while incarcerated. The court of appeals affirmed the denial. USCOURTS-SEL-01

  • Observed at 17:10:56 Eastern time ET
    USA v. Pedro Santacruz (opens in a new tab)
    Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-ca11-25-11943 / USCOURTS-ca11-25-11943-0

    FAPD-AI: Pedro Santacruz appealed a 187-month sentence imposed upon resentencing for methamphetamine conspiracy and possession with intent to distribute offenses, challenging the denial of safety-valve relief, the attribution of drug weight between him and his codefendant, and the substantive reasonableness of his sentence. The court of appeals affirmed, finding the district court did not err in denying safety-valve relief because it indicated it would impose the same sentence regardless, the law-of-the-case doctrine barred reconsideration of drug-weight attribution, and the sentence was substantively reasonable in light of applicable sentencing factors. USCOURTS-SEL-01

  • Observed at 17:10:56 Eastern time ET
    USA v. Ricardo Verdin-Castro (opens in a new tab)
    Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-ca11-25-12242 / USCOURTS-ca11-25-12242-0

    FAPD-AI: Ricardo Verdin-Castro appealed the denial of a sentence reduction under 18 U.S.C. § 3582(c)(2) based on Amendment 821 to the Sentencing Guidelines, which provided for a two-level decrease in offense level. The district court denied the reduction, finding that the 18 U.S.C. § 3553(a) factors did not support a reduction given the seriousness of his cocaine trafficking offense involving 708 kilograms. The Eleventh Circuit affirmed the denial, holding that the district court acted within its discretion in assigning substantial weight to the nature and seriousness of the offense. USCOURTS-SEL-01

  • Observed at 17:10:55 Eastern time ET
    In Re: Chiquita Brands International, Inc., et al (opens in a new tab)
    Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-ca11-24-14039 / USCOURTS-ca11-24-14039-0

    FAPD-AI: Paul Wolf appealed an order enforcing a charging lien against his attorney's fee share from a $12.8 million settlement in a case where Colombian plaintiffs sued Chiquita Brands for allegedly paying a paramilitary group over $1.7 million to suppress labor unrest. The Conrad & Scherer law firm sought to enforce the charging lien based on services rendered before being discharged from representation. The court dismissed the appeal for lack of jurisdiction, holding that orders enforcing charging liens are not appealable under the collateral-order doctrine. USCOURTS-SEL-01

  • Observed at 17:10:54 Eastern time ET
    Hubert Acevedo v. Alex de la Portilla, et al (opens in a new tab)
    Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-ca11-24-12650 / USCOURTS-ca11-24-12650-0

    FAPD-AI: Hubert Acevedo, Police Chief of Miami, wrote a whistleblowing memo to city officials and law enforcement describing how city commissioners improperly involved themselves in police investigations and attempted to weaponize the police department to advance personal agendas. After the memo leaked to the media, the commissioners voted to investigate the alleged misconduct and terminated Acevedo, who sued for retaliation in violation of the First Amendment. The court affirmed that the defendant commissioners were not entitled to qualified immunity on the retaliation claim, but reversed as to the city manager. USCOURTS-SEL-01

    Air Plan Approval; Kentucky; Louisville Area Limited Maintenance Plan for the 1997 8-Hour Ozone NAAQS (opens in a new tab)
    Federal Register · govinfo API · ENVIRONMENTAL PROTECTION AGENCY · FR-2026-08-27 / 2026-17501

    official summary: The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA or Agency) is proposing to approve a State Implementation Plan (SIP) revision submitted by the Commonwealth of Kentucky through the Energy and Environment Cabinet (Cabinet) on behalf of the Louisville Metro Air Pollution Control District (District) via a letter dated June 3, 2024. The SIP revision consists of a Limited Maintenance Plan (LMP) for the Kentucky portion of the bi-state Louisville, Kentucky-Indiana 1997 8-hour ozone maintenance area (the “bi-state Louisville Area”). The Kentucky portion of the bi-state Louisville Area includes the Bullitt, Jefferson, and Oldham Counties of Kentucky (the “Louisville Area”). The EPA is proposing to approve the Louisville Area's LMP because it provides for the maintenance of the 1997 8-hour ozone National Ambient Air Quality Standards (NAAQS) within the bi-state Louisville Area through the end of the second 10-year portion of the maintenance period. The effect of this proposed action would be to make certain commitments related to maintenance of the 1997 8-hour ozone NAAQS in the Louisville Area federally enforceable as part of the Kentucky SIP. FR-SEL-02

    Air Plan Approval; Mississippi; 2010 1-Hour SO 2 NAAQS Transport Infrastructure (opens in a new tab)
    Federal Register · govinfo API · ENVIRONMENTAL PROTECTION AGENCY · FR-2026-08-27 / 2026-17503

    official summary: Pursuant to the Federal Clean Air Act (CAA or the Act), the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA or Agency) is proposing to approve a State Implementation Plan (SIP) revision submitted by the State of Mississippi, through the Mississippi Department of Environmental Quality (MDEQ), on January 27, 2022, for the purpose of complying with the “good neighbor” provision of the CAA for the 2010 1-hour sulfur dioxide (SO 2 ) primary National Ambient Air Quality Standard (NAAQS). The good neighbor provision requires each State's implementation plan to contain adequate provisions prohibiting the interstate transport of air pollution in amounts that will contribute significantly to nonattainment, or interfere with maintenance, of a NAAQS in any other State. In this proposed rulemaking, the EPA is proposing to determine that Mississippi will not contribute significantly to nonattainment or interfere with maintenance of the 2010 1-hour SO 2 primary NAAQS in any other State. Therefore, the EPA is proposing to approve the January 27, 2022, SIP revision as meeting the requirements of the good neighbor provision for the 2010 1-hour SO 2 primary NAAQS. FR-SEL-02

    Federal Register · govinfo API · DEPARTMENT OF JUSTICE · FR-2026-08-27 / 2026-17531

    official summary: The Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) issues this temporary order to schedule 1-(1-(1-(4-bromophenyl)ethyl)piperidin-4-yl)-5,6-dichloro-1,3-dihydro-2 H -benzo[ d ]imidazol-2-one (commonly known as 5,6-dichloro brorphine or SR-14968); 5,6-dichloro-1-(1-(4-chlorobenzyl)piperidin-4-yl)-1,3-dihydro-2 H -benzo[ d ]imidazol-2-one (commonly known as 5,6-dichloro desmethylchlorphine or SR-17018); 3-(3-(1-(1-(4-chlorophenyl)ethyl)piperidin-4-yl)-2-oxo-2,3-dihydro-1 H -benzo[ d ]imidazol-1-yl)propanenitrile (commonly known as N -propionitrile chlorphine or cychlorphine); and 8-(1-(4-chlorophenyl)ethyl)-1-phenyl-1,3,8-triazaspiro[4.5]decan-4-one (commonly known as spirochlorphine or R-6890), including their isomers, esters, ethers, salts, and salts of isomers, esters, and ethers, whenever the existence of such isomers, esters, ethers, and salts is possible, to schedule I under the Controlled Substances Act.     Schedules of Controlled Substances: Placement of Cipepofol in Schedule IV (opens in a new tab)
    Federal Register · govinfo API · DEPARTMENT OF JUSTICE · FR-2026-08-27 / 2026-17536

    official summary: On May 29, 2026, the United States Food and Drug Administration (FDA) approved a new drug application for Cypsedo (cipepofol) for induction of general anesthesia in adults undergoing surgery. The Department of Health and Human Services provided the Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) with a scheduling recommendation to place cipepofol, chemically known as 2-[(1 R )-1-cyclopropylethyl]-6-isopropylphenol, in schedule IV of the Controlled Substances Act (CSA). In accordance with the CSA, as amended by the Improving Regulatory Transparency for New Medical Therapies Act, DEA is hereby issuing an interim final rule placing cipepofol in schedule IV of the CSA. FR-SEL-01

    Airworthiness Directives; Airbus SAS Airplanes (opens in a new tab)
    Federal Register · govinfo API · DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORTATION · FR-2026-08-27 / 2026-17551

    official summary: The FAA is superseding Airworthiness Directive (AD) 2024-25-06, which applied to all Airbus SAS Model A318 and A320 series airplanes; and Model A319-111, -112, -113, -114, -115, -131, -132, -133, -151N, -153N, and -171N airplanes; and Model A321-111, -112, -131, -211, -212, -213, -231, -232, -251N, -252N, -253N, -271N, -272N, -251NX, -252NX, -253NX, -271NX, -272NX, and -253NY airplanes. AD 2024-25-06 required repetitive inspections of the main landing gear (MLG) door actuators and, depending on findings, accomplishment of applicable corrective actions, and prohibited the installation of affected parts. Since the FAA issued AD 2024-05-06, the FAA determined that replacing the MLG door actuators is necessary to address the unsafe condition, and the applicability and definition of an affected part must be expanded. This AD continues to require the actions in AD 2024-25-06, requires replacing affected parts with serviceable parts, and expands the applicability and definition of an affected part. The FAA is issuing this AD to address the unsafe condition on these products. FR-SEL-01

    Airworthiness Directives; Airbus SAS Airplanes (opens in a new tab)
    Federal Register · govinfo API · DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORTATION · FR-2026-08-27 / 2026-17552

    official summary: The FAA is adopting a new airworthiness directive (AD) for certain Airbus SAS Model A320-211, -212, -214, -216, -231, -232, and -233 airplanes; and Model A321-111, -112, -131, -211, -212, -213, -231, and -232 airplanes. This AD was prompted by a fatigue test that identified cracks in the forward and aft upper corner of the bulk cargo door. This AD requires a rototest inspection for cracks and applicable on-condition actions. The FAA is issuing this AD to address the unsafe condition on these products. FR-SEL-01

  • Observed at 01:58:49 Eastern time ET
    Airworthiness Directives; The Boeing Company Airplanes (opens in a new tab)
    Federal Register · govinfo API · DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORTATION · FR-2026-08-27 / 2026-17553

    official summary: The FAA is adopting a new airworthiness directive (AD) for certain The Boeing Company Model 787-8, 787-9, and 787-10 airplanes. This AD was prompted by a Boeing investigation for manufacturing errors and excessive preload forces at the lower side of body (SOB) splice plates common to the lower outboard wing skins. That investigation concluded that shim gaps may have exceeded engineering allowances, and high pull up forces on the components may cause fatigue cracks to form at the fastener holes. This AD requires, depending on configuration, repetitive ultrasonic (UT) inspections at certain splice plates, rear spar terminal fittings, lower chords, front spar terminal fittings, and jack pads for any cracks; repetitive detailed inspections (DET) of certain splice plates for any cracks; and applicable on-condition actions. The FAA is issuing this AD to address the unsafe condition on these products. FR-SEL-01
